description: Build a test plan, record results and remedial action, then review what worked and what to improve.
hero_image_caption: A developer reviewing test results on a screen with a checklist and notes beside them.
content_html:
Why Testing Matters

Once an AR prototype has been built, it must be tested before it can be presented to a client or used by a real audience. Testing proves that the prototype works as intended — that every trigger fires correctly, every layer appears as designed, and every information output reaches the user. Without testing, faults may only be discovered when the product is in front of its audience, which is too late to fix them easily.

Testing is carried out using a test plan. A test plan makes the process systematic: every feature is checked in a defined order, results are recorded, and any problem found is linked directly to the action taken to fix it. A well-written test plan also provides evidence of the testing process — important for coursework assessment where the process is marked alongside the product.

The Test Plan Structure

Every row in a test plan covers one specific test. The required columns are:

  • Test number — a unique identifier so tests can be referenced easily when discussing remedial action or retesting.
  • What is being tested — a precise description of the feature or function under test (e.g. “marker trigger 1 fires layer 1 content”).
  • Expected result — what should happen when the test is run correctly. This is written before the test is carried out.
  • Actual result — what actually happened when the test was run. This is recorded after testing.
  • Remedial action — what was changed to fix any mismatch between expected and actual results. If the test passed, this column is left blank or marked “none required”.
Key Fact

A test plan has five columns: test number — what is being tested — expected result — actual result — remedial action. The expected result is always written before testing; the actual result and remedial action are filled in after.

Types of Testing

AR prototypes require two distinct types of testing, which serve different purposes.

Technical testing is carried out by the developer to verify that the AR prototype functions as built. This includes checking that every trigger correctly activates the right content, that layers load and display without errors, that interactive elements (swipe, click, voice) respond as expected, and that information outputs — audio, images, video, text — all appear in the correct format and quality.

Technical testing is methodical: the developer works through the test plan row by row, running each test in a controlled way and recording the outcome. Where the actual result does not match the expected result, remedial action is required. After the fix is applied, the affected test must be run again to confirm the problem has been resolved — this is called retesting.

User testing is carried out by members of the target audience. It checks whether the product is easy to understand and use, not just whether it works technically. Users may find the interface confusing, the text too small, or the trigger images unclear — problems that a developer testing their own work might not notice.

Feedback from user testing is recorded and used to identify further remedial actions. If users consistently struggle with a particular step, that step needs redesigning. User testing is therefore most effective when it uses people who genuinely represent the target audience — testing a product designed for primary school children with a group of adults will not give useful results.

Key Fact

Technical testing is carried out by the developer — it checks the prototype works as built. User testing is carried out by the target audience — it checks the prototype is easy to use and meets their needs. Both are required; one cannot replace the other.

When to Carry Out Remedial Action

Remedial action is taken whenever the actual result of a test does not match the expected result. The action taken is recorded in the test plan alongside the original test, so there is a clear audit trail. After remedial action, the affected feature must be retested and the new actual result recorded. Remedial action is part of normal development — finding problems during testing is the point of the exercise. A prototype with no remedial action recorded may simply mean the developer did not test thoroughly enough.

Reviewing the Process

After testing is complete, the developer carries out a formal review of the entire AR prototype project. This review evaluates how well the process went, not just how good the final product is. A thorough review covers four areas.

First: the effectiveness of the processes followed. Did the planning tools (flowcharts, storyboards, wireframes) produce useful design documentation? Was the design documentation actually used during the build, or was it produced just to tick a box?

Second: the effectiveness of the tools and techniques used. Did the AR authoring software perform well? Were the right design tools chosen for the task, or would different tools have worked better?

Third: does the prototype meet the defined purpose? Going back to the original purpose and user requirements written at the planning stage, does the finished prototype do what it was supposed to do? If not, why not?

Fourth: lessons learnt — a reflection on what the developer would do differently if they started the project again. Lessons learnt are not a list of failures: they are evidence of professional reflection and improved practice for next time.
exam_tip_html: In an extended response question about testing or reviewing, avoid listing points without connecting them. Examiners reward chains of reasoning: “User testing is important because target users may find the interface confusing even if it works technically, which means that technical testing alone is not enough to confirm the prototype is fit for purpose.” Questions that ask you to ‘discuss’ or ‘evaluate’ require a balanced argument and a supported conclusion — without a justified final judgement, you will not reach the top mark band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A test plan records test number, what is being tested, expected result, actual result and remedial action — it is the evidence trail for the testing process.
  • Technical testing checks the prototype works as built; user testing checks it works for the target audience — both are required.
  • Reviewing the process means evaluating the effectiveness of processes and tools, whether the prototype meets its purpose, and identifying lessons learnt for future improvement.

practice_questions.text:
Which column in a test plan is completed BEFORE the test is carried out?
A. Actual result
B. Remedial action
C. Expected result
D. Test number
practice_questions.marks: C — Expected result. (1 mark for correct letter or full term. Note: D, test number, is also written before testing but its purpose is as an identifier, not as a prediction of what will happen.)

practice_questions.text: State one type of testing a developer carries out on an AR prototype.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: technical testing OR user testing. Both are acceptable.

practice_questions.text: Outline the purpose of a test plan when testing an AR prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): States that a test plan provides a structured record (1) that allows the developer to systematically check every feature and record what happens so problems can be identified and fixed (1).
Secure (2): Two of: systematic approach / records expected and actual results / links problems to remedial action / provides evidence of the testing process.
Developing (1): States only 'to check it works' without explaining the role of the structured plan.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between technical testing and user testing of an AR prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Clearly contrasts both types on at least one dimension — e.g. who carries it out (developer vs target audience) and what it checks (technical function vs ease of use).
Secure (1–2): One clear point of contrast, e.g. developer carries out technical testing / target audience carries out user testing.
Developing (1): Names both types without clearly stating a difference.
Emerging (0): No relevant contrast made.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a developer should carry out user testing as well as technical testing on an AR prototype.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): States that technical testing only checks the prototype works as built (1) AND identifies that user testing reveals usability problems that developers may not notice themselves (1) AND uses a connective to explain the consequence, e.g. 'this means that without user testing, the prototype may be technically correct but confusing for its target audience' (1).
Secure (2): Two connected points clearly contrasting what each type of testing achieves.
Developing (1): States that user testing is useful without explaining why technical testing alone is insufficient.
Emerging (0): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text: A student has completed their AR prototype for a client brief. They have carried out technical testing and found that the main trigger does not fire consistently. Discuss how the student should respond to this finding and what they should record in their test plan. You should also consider how the review of the project should address this issue.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): Clear understanding of both testing and reviewing. Testing response: remedial action column is completed with the fix applied (e.g. redesign the trigger image to remove blurred elements or blank space) (1); the affected test is then retested and the new actual result is recorded (1); this process repeats until expected and actual results match (1). Reviewing response: the review should assess whether the design documentation for the trigger was adequate (1); consider whether the trigger design tool (e.g. visualisation diagram) gave sufficient guidance (1); identify the lesson learnt (e.g. 'in future, the trigger image should be reviewed against quality criteria before building begins') (1). Reaches a supported conclusion about whether the trigger failure reveals a design process issue or a build issue (1). Evidence and reasoning embedded throughout. Accurate use of terminology throughout (1).
Secure (5–7): Good understanding of either the testing or reviewing section, with some coverage of both. Remedial action and retesting discussed. Review mentions lessons learnt. Missing full depth in at least one area.
Developing (3–4): Describes what remedial action means or what a review should cover but does not connect the specific trigger problem to the required response. Limited use of correct terminology.
Emerging (1–2): Some relevant knowledge present but response is largely generic or disorganised. No structured argument.

knowledge_checks.q: A developer discovers that an AR layer does not load when the trigger is scanned. What should they do next?
options: Delete the test from the plan
Record the actual result and carry out remedial action
Mark the test as passed and move on
Run user testing before fixing the problem

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of testing checks whether the AR prototype is easy to use from the perspective of the target audience?
After carrying out remedial action on a failed test, the developer must _____ the test to confirm the problem has been resolved.
The review of an AR prototype project should include an evaluation of whether the prototype meets the _____ purpose defined at the planning stage.
Match each test plan column to its description.
right: The change made to fix a problem found during testing
What happens when the test is run
What should happen — written before the test is carried out

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five columns in an AR prototype test plan.
flashcard_questions.a: Test number, what is being tested, expected result, actual result, remedial action.

flashcard_questions.q: When is the 'expected result' column completed in a test plan?
flashcard_questions.a: Before the test is carried out.

flashcard_questions.q: What is technical testing of an AR prototype?
flashcard_questions.a: Testing by the developer to verify the prototype functions as built.

flashcard_questions.q: What does technical testing check in an AR prototype?
flashcard_questions.a: That triggers fire, layers appear, and information outputs display correctly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is user testing of an AR prototype?
flashcard_questions.a: Testing by target audience members to check the product is easy to use.

flashcard_questions.q: When should remedial action be carried out?
flashcard_questions.a: When the actual result does not match the expected result.

flashcard_questions.q: What must happen after remedial action is taken?
flashcard_questions.a: The affected test must be retested and the new result recorded.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four areas covered in a review of an AR prototype project.
flashcard_questions.a: Effectiveness of processes, effectiveness of tools, whether purpose is met, lessons learnt.

flashcard_questions.q: What are 'lessons learnt' in a project review?
flashcard_questions.a: A reflection on what the developer would do differently to improve next time.

flashcard_questions.q: What is remedial action in the context of AR testing?
flashcard_questions.a: A change made to the prototype to correct a problem discovered during testing.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is user testing carried out by the target audience rather than the developer?
flashcard_questions.a: Users find usability issues the developer may not notice testing their own work.

glossary_terms.definition: A structured document listing each test to be run, with columns for the test number, what is being tested, expected result, actual result, and any remedial action taken.
Testing carried out by the developer to verify that the technical functions of the AR prototype work correctly — triggers fire, layers appear, outputs display.
Testing carried out by members of the target audience to check that the AR prototype is easy to use and meets the users' needs.
A change made to an AR prototype to correct a problem discovered during testing.
